subtopic: DISARMAMENT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DISARMAMENT
subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPLY TO PREMIER KHRUSHCHEV
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my reply has now been transmitted to the message from Chairman Khrushchev in which he proposed that heads of government should attend the opening meetings of the disarmament commission when it begins its work in Geneva on March 14. I should now like to table that reply so that hon. members will have it before them.
I made clear to Mr. Khrushchev that I welcomed the spirit in which his proposal appears to have been made, since it would seem to indicate that the Soviet union attaches importance to the forthcoming disarmament negotiations. The Canadian government believes that this conference must be
the occasion for the greatest effort which the nations of the world have yet made toward a solution of the pressing problems in the disarmament field. Fortunately a good basis has been laid for the conference in the form of an agreement on general principles. The first task will be to convert these principles into practical measures of disarmament.
In my reply to Mr. Khrushchev I have said I believe the foreign ministers should be present at the outset to give additional direction and impetus to the work of the conference.
As these problems affect all countries, and depend in some degree on all countries for their solution, there is a significant role in these discussions for the middle and smaller powers. The difficult problems requiring solution may in the end yield only to direct conversation among the heads of government.
I have therefore repeated to Chairman Khrushchev what I told the house last Monday, namely that whenever the presence of heads of government is considered to be advantageous, I should personally be ready to attend such a meeting. Should efforts for disarmament meet with even partial success, then a measure of confidence will have been established which might enable other critical problems between east and west to be dealt with.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISARMAMENT
subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPLY TO PREMIER KHRUSHCHEV
speechtext: Has the Prime Minister leave to table the document referred to?

subtopic: DISARMAMENT
subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPLY TO PREMIER KHRUSHCHEV
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISARMAMENT

subtopic: DISARMAMENT
subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPLY TO PREMIER KHRUSHCHEV

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DISARMAMENT
subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPLY TO PREMIER KHRUSHCHEV
speechtext:
I think all hon. members in the house will support the position of the Prime Minister and the government in respect of this matter, in emphasizing in the first place the importance of the conference in question and the desirability of doing everything possible at the conference to make progress toward peace rather than allowing it to become merely an exercise in propaganda. I think also the Prime Minister was wise in his emphasis that at the early stages of a conference of this kind it is better to leave these matters in the hands of the ministers particularly concerned. I notice Mr. Khrushchev refers to them as bureaucrats; I am sure

Inquiries of the Ministry that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will deny that suggestion. Then if any progress is made at the foreign ministers level, and we all hope that there will be progress, that would be the time to consider elevating, if you like, the representations to the heads of government level.
But as the Prime Minister has pointed out, surely it is important to get ahead with the business of disarmament, and at this commission of 18, with certain principles to guide it which have been agreed upon at the United Nations, there is now an opportunity for progress. Then if and when you get results, that will be the time to bring in the heads of government to continue and perhaps to finalize that progress.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for St. John's East inquired whether I had been aware that a statement was made in St. John's yesterday by the premier of Newfoundland to the effect that Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation anticipates laying off 700 of their personnel at the Wabana mines, Bell island. I made inquiries through our unemployment insurance commission and they have reported to me as follows:
In December last DOSCO announced that failure of buyers to meet 1961 contracts and reluctance of the market to contract for 1962 would necessitate a cut back in 1962 production. At that time it was thought the work force of some 1,600 would be reduced by 500 during January. This reduction did not occur, however, and on January 28 the mines closed completely for a period that was to run for seven weeks.
The premier of Newfoundland is reported to have announced yesterday in the house of assembly that 700 Wabana workers would lose their jobs almost immediately. In making this statement the premier is reported to have reviewed his negotiations with Dominion Coal and Steel Company to avert the lay-off. These negotiations, he stated, were not successful. It would appear that this lay-off would become effective at the end of the current seven week shutdown. The premier is reported to have had confirmation of the lay-off from Mr. Fairley, the president of DOSCO, but the company did not issue a statement itself.
The prospect of other work in the immediate area for laid off miners is not good and because of their long association with the area, difficulties have been encountered in moving these workers to employment elsewhere.
The root of the Wabana mines difficulties appears to lie in loss of European markets and increased use of ore from Labrador by the DOSCO plant at Sydney. Loss of European markets has been mentioned both by Premier Smallwood and the company. However, as far as we can ascertain no public announcement has been made by either concerning increased use of Labrador ore at the Sydney plant.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: OBLIGATIONS OF MEMBERS RESPECTING CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in the light of the fact that certain member nations are not paying their contributions in support of the peace keeping operations of the United Nations, if he could tell us what the situation is now as a result of the decision of the sixteenth assembly, when it was decided to ask the international court of justice for an advisory opinion as to the legal obligations of all member states to these peace keeping operations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: OBLIGATIONS OF MEMBERS RESPECTING CONTRIBUTIONS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The general assembly, by resolution dated December 20, 1961, requested the international court of justice to give an advisory opinion on the question as to whether the expenditures authorized by the general assembly in relation to the financing of the United Nations operations in the Congo and the United Nations emergency force constitute expenses of the organization within the meaning of article 17, paragraph 2 of the charter of the United Nations.
By an order of the president of the international court of justice dated December 27, 1961, member states of the United Nations have been invited to submit written statements in relation to this question, and the order has fixed February 20, 1962, as the time limit within which such statements should be filed.
In accordance with the opportunity thus made available to member states, the government of Canada will within the next few days be submitting a written statement setting out its views regarding this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS EXTENDING PAYMENTS TO CERTAIN GROUPS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I spoke at some length both on the resolution and at
second reading stage. I feel there is nothing further to be said in a general way with respect to these amendments.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the minister that we have had already a lengthy discussion on this bill and that no good purpose would be served by prolonging the discussion at this stage. However, I wish to assure the committee that I had no intention of introducing a partisan note in this debate, as the minister appeared to allege in his remarks on second reading yesterday. We in the Liberal party have been fully in support of this bill. We fully support the payments being made to the groups concerned under this legislation.
There is only one small point of disagreement between hon. gentlemen opposite and those on this side of the house. It concerns not the terms of the bill or the amount of the allowances but the manner in which they are going to be paid. Since we are going to recognize the worth of the services rendered by these groups who served in theatres of war we feel we should accord them the same recognition we accord other groups who served in the armed forces. In other words we should accord these groups the status of veterans.
That is the proper function of an opposition. We are not here to agree with everything the government does. We are here to point out ways in which legislation can be improved, and that is all we have sought to do.
The hon. member sounds like a professor.

I would ask the hon. member to keep quiet for a moment or two. It has been pointed out by some hon. members that the terms of this agreement are quite satisfactory to the Newfoundland foresters. Perhaps that is so. However, that consideration does not relieve us of our responsibility to the people of Canada to put this legislation on the statute books in the very best possible form. That is our function here, namely to criticize legislation and find ways and means of improving it. No matter of an agreement by anyone can relieve us of that responsibility. Although, as some hon. members have pointed out, the president of the Newfoundland foresters' association made some remarks which could be interpreted to mean that he was satisfied with it, even in the passage that was quoted from his brief to support that argument that gentleman indicated that their first choice was that they should be brought under the veterans charter.
However, apart from all that, I wish the house to consider that more than the Newfoundland foresters are involved. There are the merchant navy personnel to be considered.
Civilian War Pensions
and they are far more numerous. We have no assurance at all that they are satisfied to have their status as veterans overlooked. In any event, I think we have pressed the point far enough and I do not intend to carry it any further.
I have some questions to ask on the various clauses as they come up for consideration, but since the minister last night indicated that he had gone into the reasons why these people should not be brought under the War Veterans Allowance Act, and since he has not informed the house of these reasons, I think perhaps he might like to do so now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?
Carried.
Is no reply to be given?

Clause agreed to.
Clause 2 agreed to.
On clause 3-Definitions.

On clause 3, will the minister explain what changes, if any, are involved in this clause? The explanation says that it is consequential upon the adding of part XI to the act. However, if we read it we find it states that these claims for pension and so on are now to be adjudicated in a like manner to those under the Pension Act.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I think we just passed clause 2.
No.
What the hon. member is dealing with is not clause 3 but rather section 3 of clause 2.
I was not aware that clause 2 had been passed, Mr. Chairman. I would ask that the committee revert to clause 2, as it was carried very rapidly.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Under the circumstances I think it would be permissible for the hon. member to proceed.

What I am asking the minister to do is to explain to the committee just what changes are involved in this wording or in this subsection which states that all claims for pensions, allowances and compensation are going to be dealt with and adjudicated upon in a like manner as claims under the Pension Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The answer is simply that this section is the same as the section now reads in the present act except for the part underlined, which had to be inserted because of the addition of part XI. Hence the act stands as it stood previously with regard to parts I to

Civilian War Pensions
X which are at present included in the act, and part XI is dealt with as set out in the next section.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is perhaps a difficulty here. Clause 3 is a long one. The committee may wish to discuss it item by item or may wish to pass it all as a single clause. Has the hon. member for Kootenay West some observations to make on clause 3?

Yes. I was going to ask the minister for an explanation of section 68 in clause 3. Section 68 reads as follows:
68. No allowance shall be paid to any person who in world war II served
(a)	in enemy forces,
(b)	in an enemy ship, or
(c)	in war service groups associated with forces of the enemy.
Will he explain why it is necessary to put that clause in this bill? It seems to be somewhat unusual.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I find it a little bit difficult to follow the hon. member's remarks because of other considerations going on in the chamber. Will the hon. member repeat his question?

Yes, certainly. I am asking a question on section 68 on page 4 of the bill, which reads as follows:
68. No allowance shall be paid to any person who in world war II served
(a)	in enemy forces,
(b)	in an enemy ship, or
(c)	in war service groups associated with forces of the enemy.
I wonder why it is necessary to put such a clause in a bill like this.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
So there will be no misunderstanding at all may I say that it is a repetition of a section in the War Veterans Allowance Act, namely section 9, which reads as follows:
No allowance shall be paid to any person who served in enemy forces in world war II.
It seems to be unusual and unnecessary in a sense. I would not expect them to get an allowance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 3 carry?

No. On clause 69 or section 69, whichever is the way in which you are dealing with it, I have a question to ask. Perhaps I might take sections 69 and 70 together. Does this mean that the groups mentioned in this legislation will be entitled to all the benefits under the War Veterans Allowance Act? If not, that benefits will be withheld?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: This is the section which bears on the board's power to adjudicate all claims just as they do now under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
Is everyone in these categories entitled to every kind of allowance to which persons are entitled under the War Veterans Allowance Act? If not, what difference is there?

I think that matter is of the essence in our discussion in committee of the whole. With respect to clause 3 the explanatory note states as follows:
The allowances payable under the proposed amendment are similar to the allowances paid to veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has been more specific than that. The word "similar" is not quite adequate for a member of parliament who is looking at pages 2 to 7, as I recall it, on which appear sections which involve changes with respect to this legislation. I think the minister and his learned parliamentary secretary should indicate to us specifically just what is and what is not similar to the War Veterans Allowance Act so far as these new categories are concerned, because the situation is unique. The bill is not going to the veterans affairs committee for the minute and careful examination that normally always follows after any legislation concerning veterans has been introduced in the house. The government established a standing committee on veterans affairs, but that committee is not being asked to peruse this legislation. This bill is an important matter to a great number of people who have been denied classification as a veteran as requested yesterday by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. But that having been denied, what are the additional distinctions? The word "similar" in the explanatory note is not quite adequate in order to assure us that there will be equality. "Similar" is not the same as "same" and "equal".

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I say to the hon. member who has just spoken that if he wishes this legislation to be delayed and referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs, let him say so right now. It will mean postponing consideration of the bill for perhaps two weeks, because it takes quite a while to arrange for representatives of the various veterans organizations to come to Otawa. If he is suggesting that type of delay, let him say so.
That is not delay.
It would not bother me.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On the other hand, if the hon. member wants to go ahead with the legislation, let us proceed as we are right now.

Mr. Chairman, I have great respect for the minister. Over the years I think all members of the veterans affairs committee have proven that they are friends of the veterans, and certainly the minister has proven himself to be one. However, in circumstances of this kind the man who receives all the information and who has the staff to learn all the unsatisfied criticisms is the person who, as in the past, must report to this committee what criticisms he has received that are not satisfied by the legislation.
I am not satisfied that the word "similar" is entirely adequate. In the present circumstances I am perfectly prepared to take the word of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who has been a good friend of the veterans as have his predecessors in all political parties. I simply want to make sure while we are making what I think is a very desirable advance that I can never be accused of having been lacking in proper criticism and not having done as much as I could when the legislation was before the house.
The word "similar" is not entirely satisfactory to me. I know the minister has received briefs on this matter from all the veterans organizations over a period of a great many years. I simply want him to take the opposition and others into his confidence and tell us to what extent there may be differences between what a regular veteran gets and what these other categories who served this country well in wartime are likely to get under this legislation which I am sure he has much pleasure in introducing at this session, as he should have.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: If we restrict ourselves to matters which are relevant to the bill I am perfectly happy, and I know the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River will do that. The word "similar" was used because there is one slight difference and we wanted to be absolutely frank about the thing. The slight difference is that we have not brought into this particular bill section 4 of the War Veterans Allowance Act, which permits allowances to employable veterans. That particular section has almost fallen into disuse over the years, and it did not seem advisable to introduce it into this bill. As a matter of fact the veterans rely on section 3, where casual earnings come into the picture, and section 4 has fallen into disuse. There are now only 93 recipients under section 4 out of 72,000 people who come under the War Veterans Allowance Act.

There is no necessity to labour the matter, but I should like to ask whether those persons who will be eligible to receive the benefits of this act will receive
Civilian War Pensions
the same service, the same processing and the same results in principle and practice as recipients under the War Veterans Allowance Act in general.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

From the same board.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, from the same war veterans allowance board.

I should like to ask one question about the 93 persons who are receiving an allowance under section 4. Are those all awards that were made some considerable time ago? Can the minister assure us that no new awards are being made under section 4?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am so informed. No new awards have been made under section 4. They were all made several years ago.

Then it would be quite precise to say that so far as veterans are concerned, section 4 would not be used for anyone coming under the War Veterans Allowance Act, either those previously qualified or those who would now qualify?

I should like to ask the minister whether the 365-day clause will apply in qualifying for these benefits.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Some of them were in France.

If they served less than 365 days in world war I would they be entitled to any benefits under the legislation before us?

Perhaps I should explain my question a little further. I was thinking about veterans who served in the first world war who had less than 365 days in the service and could not therefore qualify for benefit, but who may have enlisted in a forestry unit or some other unit in world war II. speechtext: The world war II service would make them eligible.

I am going to risk having
the chairman rule me out of order by asking the minister if he does not believe the time has come to remove the 365-day discrimination with respect to veterans of world war I.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Are you the chairman now?

As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, as my hon. friend from Laurier has observed, I do not think we should permit the minister to usurp the functions of the Chair. It is not for the minister to say whether or not a question is out of order. Your Honour allowed me to ask the question, and I feel the minister ought to answer it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I understand correctly the minister has given an answer.
Well, the answer will be very unsatisfactory to a large number of veterans.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: If I may speak to the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I would say we are not dealing with veterans, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate knows. As was decided yesterday, under this bill we are dealing with persons under the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Speaking to the point of order, I would say discussion must be related to the provisions of the bill.

On page 6 of the bill I find this paragraph:
For the purposes of this section
(a) "dangerous waters" means such oceans, seas or waters as the board may prescribe:
Does this give the board discretionary powers to determine what shall be considered as dangerous waters?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The whole purpose is to give discretion to the board, and rightly so; because if we put a limitation in the bill then somebody somewhere may come to us and say he had served in waters which for 40 years we had thought were not dangerous but he might prove to us that they were. This provision does give discretion to the war veterans allowance board.
What are the over-all rights of the minister, in regard to this point, to go beyond what the decision of the board might have been?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There are no rights in the minister to go beyond the decision of the board.
I am interested in this question of dangerous waters, because it seems to me that we are giving the board powers in this legislation which it did not have before. Is that the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, that is not the case. Under section 38, subsection (c) paragraph (ii), the war veterans allowance board has the right to determine places, zones or areas as the board may prescribe, to use the words that are in the act. It is, therefore, the same type of discretionary power given to the board.
The minister cannot alter that decision of the war veterans allowance board?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. I do not see why he
should.

I recall pursuing this question in the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs, I think it was at the last session. If 1 recall correctly I was told by the witness who appeared on behalf of the board that the board was governed in its definition of dangerous waters by a ruling that had been handed down by the Department of Justice. I gather that under the provisions of this bill the board is not required to be bound by any decision handed down by the Department of Justice in this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

allowance board on behalf of a person who had served in waters just off the coast of Newfoundland, between Bell island and the mainland, in which submarines had torpedoed several ore boats. I pointed out that these were certainly dangerous waters.
I pointed out, too, that in the area between Port aux Basques and Sydney our ferry had been torpedoed. These were, therefore, dangerous waters. I am trying to make sure that the board does have discretionary authority under this measure now to designate these as dangerous waters if they so wish.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR EXTENSION OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
This legislation was first enacted in May, 1953. It was based on the principle that the children of a war veteran were entitled to an education, and that they should not be deprived of an education because their father had been killed in action or had died of wounds or from other causes related to his war service. If we developed this principle we would see it also would apply to the children of veterans who are 100 per cent disabled. In effect it boils down
Children of War Dead Act to the ability of a veteran to finance the education of his children. When a veteran dies his family's income is reduced. It consists only of the pension and allowances received by his widow and children. This is true whether or not a veteran dies from causes that are related to his war service.
The original bill was related to those dependants who received pensions under section 13. I recall that a few years ago, when the bill was examined by a parliamentary committee, the war amputees' association pointed out that this legislation applies in cases where a pensioner may only have 10 per cent disability, provided that the cause of his death can be related to his war service. They mentioned that most of their group had a much higher disability rating. Some had 100 per cent, some 60 per cent, and they said they were handicapped in supplementing their earnings to finance the education of their children. Therefore they thought some provision should be made to amend the law so the benefits could be widened.
Now I am pleased to see that there has been a broadening of the benefits and also a clarification of the definition of "student" which may help to extend the benefits. I am also glad that the allowances have been increased, but during the short time I have had to study the bill I have found it is not clear just how far the bill goes toward meeting the wishes expressed by the Canadian Legion, the war amputees' association and other people interested in this matter. Perhaps the minister would take a few minutes to give us a broad general outline of the changes that are proposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR EXTENSION OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
There has been a great deal of interest taken by veterans associations in this particular act, the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act. That is quite understandable, but in some instances we have gone further than the representations which were made to us by the veterans associations. Up to the present time the act has been a good one, and what we now are attempting to do is to make sure that what I might call the marginal cases are taken care of more fully.
There are instances when a deserving student might be prevented from continuing and completing his course and, having launched him on that course and assisted him in it for maybe three of four years, we want to make sure that he will finish the course and then make his effective contribution to the life of the country. It was because of cases like these, where hardships have resulted when a university course was discontinued, that we have brought in these amendments. We want to be able to continue to

Children of War Dead Act assist a student when, either through illness in his family or because of some economic distress, he has had to withdraw from his educational course for a year or two but then wants to resume it. We do not want the limitation of the age factor to stand in his way. Having made a good investment we want to bring it to fruition. That is generally what we have attempted to do in the amendments here proposed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR EXTENSION OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Are the benefits still limited to the dependants of those veterans whose deaths can be directly related to their war service?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR EXTENSION OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Yes, that is still the same.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 2.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR EXTENSION OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
With particular reference to subparagraph 2 we note in the supplementary notes that this is new. Therefore on the right hand side of the amending bill we do not get the law as it has existed in statute form hitherto. This may be a very desirable provision. I have no objection to it, but I want to know what the minister has in mind; because the wording says:
The minister-
I take it at his sole discretion.
-may extend the total period for which an allowance and costs may be paid-
Does this mean one could keep a student for perhaps 20 years at Harvard, London, or any other distinguished university-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR EXTENSION OF BENEFITS
speechtext: Toronto.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR EXTENSION OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
-at the discretion of the minister? It says that if he, and I underline "he", is of the opinion that the student's progress and achievements in his course of study are such that it would be in the interest of both the student and the public to do so, he may extend the period. I cannot imagine that we would have a minister of veterans affairs who would not be responsible and who perhaps would not make a proper judgment in the interest of both the student and the public, but I think the provision pretty wide.
I should like an assurance from the minister that he does not see in this an immediate opening through which he is going to give ministerial patronage to a lot of people who have progressed a certain distance with the aid of the veterans educational allowance provisions; and that while he is in office he and he alone, without any limitation upon him could keep somebody pursuing an educational course at high levels subject only to the opinion of the minister as to that

Export Credits Insurance Act
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act to increase the maximum liability at any time ol importers under outstanding instruments the payment of which is guaranteed by the corporation under section 21A of the act, from $200,000,000 to $300,000,000; and to provide further for a certain change in connection with the administration of the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING MAXIMUM LIABILITY OF IMPORTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the bill is a short one with two clauses, the first providing for an increase in the number of directors on the board, and the second to increase by $100 million the funds available for long term export financing.
The Export Credits Insurance Corporation operates in two main fields. It provides export credits insurance to protect Canadian exporters against non-payment by foreign buyers and, second, it provides funds for long term financing. Section 14 of the act provides for a maximum liability of $200 million under which the corporation may take on risks for its own account. Under section 21 there is an additional $200 million under which the governor in council may specifically instruct the corporation to provide insurance in cases where the board of directors is of the opinion that the contract would impose on the corporation a liability for a term or an amount in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake. The risk involved in any policy issued under this section 21 is carried by the consolidated revenue fund.
In 1961 the corporation insured exports totalling $132 million, and since it started operations back in 1945 it has covered a total of more than $1 billion of export sales. This amount includes consumer goods sold all over the world on credit terms usual for the trade, which extends from cash against documents to a maximum of 180 days. It also includes capital goods sold on supplier credit terms which extend to a maximum of five years credit after delivery.
Claims paid to date total $10.5 million. The corporation does not subsidize exports, but neither is it trying to make a profit. In the long run the premiums should just cover the operating expenses and net losses. The financial statements of the corporation as at December 31, 1961, which will shortly be issued, will indicate that by and large this result has been achieved, and this has been done after insuring exports of $1 billion.
In June, 1961 the Export Credits Insurance Act was amended to provide a fund of $200 million under which long term export financing would be provided to help Canadian exporters of capital goods compete on credit terms made available by organizations in other exporting countries, such as the export-import bank of Washington. Canadian capital

goods exporters, with this backing, have been encouraged to seek orders abroad. To date contracts involving exports of $41 million have been entered into on the basis of long term financing. These contracts will involve over 5.7 million man hours of work. Contracts under negotiation for which financing has been approved in principle by cabinet total $114 million. In addition guarantees totalling $31 million have also been given which come under the $200 million ceiling. Thus, out of $200 million available, a total of $186 million has been committed.
We are more than pleased with the results which have been obtained to date by this provision of long term financing; and it is now proposed in this bill to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act, that the $200 million ceiling for long term export financing under section 21A be increased by $100 million. This will enable Canadian manufacturers of heavy capital equipment to continue to seek orders from abroad on terms which are required to secure the business.

I made some tabulations last evening on this matter. As I read the figures, total world exports in terms of United States dollars between 1956 and 1960 have increased by about 21 per cent. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-9 to amend the Railway Act.
He said: It gives me a great deal of pleasure to move the second reading of Bill No. C-9 to amend the Railway Act. It came before the house during the last session and is similar to a bill which was passed last session in connection with the Transport Act. Its purpose is to provide that representatives of the trucking industry shall have the right to make application to the board of transport commissioners for the disallowance of a competitive rate when they consider that such a rate has subjected motor vehicle operators to an undue or unreasonable prejudice or disadvantage.
A number of royal commissions of one sort or another have dealt with transportation problems in Canada and with economic problems generally. Each one of those royal commissions has pointed to the benefits which have come to Canada through having a strong, independent trucking industry. Indeed, the latest royal commission on transportation, the commission which is in the process of reporting at the present time, drew attention to the views of an earlier one in this regard. On page 48 of volume 2 of the report of the present royal commission on transportation, 1961, the following appears:
Competition from motor transportation, the main medium in competition with the railways, began to be felt by the railways in the fourth decade of the present century. Statistics on the tonnage moved by motor transportation are not available for the entire period. However, even by 1939, the expansion of the facilities in motor transportation and the competition within the motor transportation industry, according to the findings of a study undertaken for the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, had:
"resulted in diverting a substantial volume of merchandise traffic in particular from the railways.
In the endeavour to stop this diversion the railways in recent years have made many reductions in their rates for this class of traffic, they have improved their service and they have relaxed their packing requirements and lowered their minimum carload weights."
Thus the emergence of an independent trucking industry in Canada has brought
Railway Act
about savings in connection with freight movements to many people in business in this country.
On the other hand, the royal commission which was set up to study the choice of route for the railroad to the Great Slave lake had this to say about what happened when the railways operate in the absence of competition. At page 26 of volume 1 of the report of the royal commission on the Great Slave Railway, the following statement is made:
Railway monopolies sometimes produce strange results with regard to freight rates. For example, the railway companies in advocating the east route emphasized that an advantage of the east route over the west route is that from Edmonton to Waterways is an easier railway to operate than from Edmonton to Grimshaw. Both railways are operated by the same company, but notwithstanding this argument.
(a)	the railway rate on fuel oil from Edmonton to Grimshaw (the longer and more difficult route) is 55 cents per hundred pounds,
(b)	the railway rate from Edmonton to McMurray (the shorter and easier route, but the route over which there is a monopoly for over half the distance) is 99 cents per hundred pounds.
I think that in the light of the two statements I have just put on record it is clear that Canada needs a strong, independent trucking industry. I say "independent trucking industry" because of the fact that the railways have for the past few years been engaged in acquiring a large hold on the trucking industry. Indeed, the present royal commission on transportation recognizes this fact and points out at page 80 of its report:
We are satisfied that already these resources have made the two largest railway companies between them the two largest owners of truck fleets in Canada.
I believe that such a situation is not in the best interests of transportation in this country. Not only is the independent trucking industry being threatened by being taken over by purchase on the part of the railway but we have the possibility of the railways endangering that part of the industry which is left, through rate wars which could have the effect of putting the remaining independent firms out of business. This danger, also, is clearly recognized by the royal commission on transportation. At page 66 of the commission's report, the following statement appears:
Enlightened management in their own interest would not knowingly carry goods at a rate which yielded revenues below the direct out-of-pocket costs, that is, those costs directly assignable to the traffic. To persist in the practice for any considerable length of time would ruin the company. Other things being equal, the regulatory provision for minimum rate control would be redundant.
However, other things are not equal. Because of their relatively enormous size and resources, and the relative permanency of investment compared to firms engaged in other modes, the railways could create intolerable uncertainty in the

Railway Act
trucking industry by sporadic rate wars, so that an efficient trucking industry could not persist.
Further down the page it states:
The effective existence of minimum rate control on railways will not, in itself, eliminate the possibilities of rate wars either between railways and trucks, or between trucking firms. The large firm can always destroy the small if satisfied that the fruits of victory are sufficiently sweet.
Then the report goes on to define one other course that might be taken. It states:
As instruments of national policy certain exemptions from these laws were necessary.
The commission was referring to combines legislation. Then the report says:
The use of traditional exemptions for restrictive purposes should not be tolerated.
I can only assume that the railways are taking every possibility of restricting competition between transportation agencies by the purchase of trucking firms. The report continues:
Part of the economic test of restraint of competition by rate practices is to determine whether the aggregate net return to be realized from the traffic moving under the new rate exceeds the net return from traffic moving under the former rate. If this is the case, the rate is not in restraint of competition. If it is not the case, further examination may be warranted. The board of transport commissioners could be requested to supply the relevant information to the Department of Justice.
I would suggest it is very necessary that the board of transport commissioners be in a position to determine whether or not goods are moving over railway lines at compensatory rates. It seems to me it is impossible for the board to have knowledge of the exact situation with regard to every rate that is put into effect by the railway companies. Indeed, they cannot possibly begin to consider each one of them. There is provision in the Railway Act at the present time for certain safeguards. The act states that rates must be compensatory and that they must not be lower than is necessary to meet competition. The trucking industry has no status before the board of transport commissioners and as they are the main people who would be in a position to know whether rates were established at dangerous levels they are the ones who logically should have the right to appear before the board and draw to the board's attention the fact that this situation has occurred.
It may be said that having a particularly low rate benefits a particular shipper at a given time. If a trucking firm is put out of business because of that fact and the competition disappears, it seems to me it would not be very long before the rates went back up again. In fact, the very people who are entitled to appeal to the board under the present

legislation are those who would be the least likely to do so because they would benefit from the abnormally low rate.
While the purpose of all our transportation legislation should be to bring about the lowest possible rates it is also true that we wish to have established rates that are capable of being maintained and we wish to ensure that there will be a continuity of service at those rates.
The type of situation that is mentioned in the report of the royal commission, that the independent trucking industry could be easily put out of business by sporadic rate wars, is a dangerous one. On the other hand, I do not suggest that the trucking industry should be in a position to prevent the railroads from establishing the rates necessary to meet competition or rates that can be maintained at economic levels.
I do not think the board should be empowered to make any change in the rates until it has been clearly established that a given rate is uneconomic. At previous times the board did have the power to set aside a rate established by the railroad until a determination was made. The railroads objected strenuously to that, and I think properly so. However, I do not see the same objection being taken to the board having power to set aside a rate after it has been established that it is uneconomic, nor can I foresee any objection to the trucking industry being allowed to go before the board when that situation exists.
As I stated earlier this bill came before the house last session. I was pleased that the principle of the bill received endorsation in the report of the royal commission on transportation. In my remarks last year as reported at page 8141 of Hansard of September 8, 1961 I stated:
On the face of it, if two industries are on equal terms, of course free competition itself would ensure the lowest possible rate to the consumer and that is the ultimate result we want to attain. However, the conditions as between the trucking industry and the rail industry are not equal by any stretch of the imagination. For one thing, the resources of the railway are far beyond those of the average trucking firm.
I am sure you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that those words are strikingly similar to what is contained in the report of the royal commission. While the report makes no reference to the specific amendment I propose to the house, at page 177 of the report it is stated:
The acts which cover those areas of transportation where our investigations lay are chiefly the Railway Act and the Transport Act. Both of these deal almost entirely with aspects of railway regulation. Both will require careful and extensive revision in the light of changing circumstances and

particularly in the light of policy changes undertaken to adjust the loss of the monopoly position of railways in overland transportation.
The report goes on to advocate that a committee of representatives of the regulatory agencies concerned, the Department of Transport and the Department of Justice should be established to consider these matters.
I believe there is a definite sense of urgency about this matter. It is quite clear from the comments made in the report of the royal commission that the amendment I have proposed in Bill No. C-9 is necessary. One can take no other interpretation from the remarks made throughout the report than that this legislation is necessary and I hope it will commend itself to the house.

Mr. Speaker, last September I had the opportunity of speaking in support of this bill which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) is introducing again and I wish to reiterate some of the comments I made on that occasion.
To begin with we must recognize that transportation has undergone a tremendous change from the days of the early railroads. Most of our regulations governing transportation date back to the time when there was neither a trans-Canada highway nor highway transports. The only means of transportation at that time were the railroad and the horsedrawn vehicle, but one could scarcely describe the latter as a competitive mode of transportation.
We are now confronted with a situation which demands revision in our thinking with regard to transportation. We have spent millions of dollars in order to construct a highway system from coast to coast, and more millions are being spent by the federal government, by the provinces, and by the municipalities, in order to provide all-weather roads for the purpose of motor transportation which, in this modern day and age, has assumed an importance of proportions which were not envisaged when regulations were formulated by the federal Department of Transport.
The bill under discussion, if approved, will bring about recognition that this important branch of the transportation industry, trucking, exists for the purpose of serving an ever increasing number of Canadians. It should, therefore no longer be looked upon as an unimportant adjunct to our older established methods of transportation, namely the railways and lake shipping.
The trucking industry, from a very small beginning in the twenties, has now attained a status of considerable proportions, with an investment in excess of $1 billion and carrying more than 100 million tons of merchandise yearly. The Canadian trucking associations of 26207-1-58i
Railway Act
Canada in their submission to the government last June emphasized that the rapid growth of the country and the spectacular progress of technology during recent years had profoundly changed the structure of Canadian transportation services. A serious problem has been created of adjusting transportation policies to meet the new situation created by the public demand for a more efficient and up to date transportation service, such as having goods delivered to your door. This has been recognized by the royal commission on transportation.
All this bill provides is the right of appeal to the board against any discriminatory rates, and the right to be heard in open court. I am particularly keen about the passage of this bill because the lakehead cities of Fort William and Port Arthur are located approximately 850 or 900 miles from Toronto, and approximately 420 miles from Winnipeg.
As a result of the distance between the heavier centres of population, we have never received due consideration from the railways in so far as fair freight rates are concerned. I can give an example of this discrimination. The freight rate on canned goods shipped from Chatham, Ontario to Fort William is $1.57 per one hundred pounds. When a wholesaler in Fort William ships these canned goods to Geraldton or Marathon, there is a charge of $1.37 per one hundred pounds for a journey of approximately 200 miles. As I say, this came about as a result of the horizontal freight rate increases that occurred during the last ten years. It was this policy of horizontal rate increases which damaged our chances to compete with other parts of the country, and which worked to our considerable disadvantage in comparison with the eastern parts of the province of Ontario.
This unfair policy, which we hope the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation will remedy in due course, has had the effect of turning shippers to and from the lakehead to motor transport for some of their needs. It is for these cogent reasons that northwestern Ontario has suffered more than its share from unbalanced freight rates which directly or indirectly everyone must pay. Higher freight costs, I submit, have a direct relationship with higher than average unemployment.
I think we should preserve the competitive spirit in Canadian transportation. The government should preserve competition as it battles cartels and combines. An independent trucking industry should be given an opportunity to compete and survive for the benefit of all Canadians. The passing of this bill will at least give the trucking industry a

Railway Act
chance to speak and fight for itself, from which in the end no one would suffer, but rather each would enjoy the fruit of his labour.
I express the hope, Mr. Speaker, that this bill will be allowed to come to a vote. To me it does not seem to make sense that bills and resolutions should be introduced by private members when everybody knows they are going to be talked out. In my opinion, any question worthy of debate should come to a vote. I believe members should be allowed to vote on it and that they should be free to vote as they see fit without necessarily committing to any policy the government or the party to which they belong, if the majority does not desire to follow the party line. In my opinion these resolutions and bills should come to a vote. I believe the move suggested would be a popular one and that all Canadians would applaud if the government were to come out and say, "We will allow these bills and resolutions presented by private members-"

hon. member who first spoke was excellent and clear. I completely endorse everything he said.
My friend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) made reference to the changes that have taken place in recent years with respect to transportation. Perhaps in no other part of Canada has this change been more evident and more pronounced than it has been in the prairie provinces. Those hon. members who live in the west will remember the days when the railway train was a vital factor in transportation. If you lived in a small town in those days the arrival of the evening train and the unloading of the express was an event. Tremendous volumes of materials of all kinds were transported by train, and a truck was a rarity. Today the truck is perhaps the dominant factor in the transportation of a large number of items. It may be of interest to the house to know that quite recently there was a trial run of live cattle from Alberta to Toronto. This is an indication of what is happening.
In my particular area we have had and still have a large number of independent trucking companies. Some of them have failed. They may have failed through inefficiency or they may have failed through lack of a keen appreciation of their particular problem. However, some of them have failed by virtue of the intrusion of competitive trucking systems supported by large institutions.
It is the purpose of this bill, as I see it, to give some protection to these independent companies in order to make it possible for them to have recourse to a referee. It is my sincere hope that in the not too distant future we may see on the statute books of Canada legislation of this type.

It disturbs me greatly that a large crown corporation such as the C.N.R. can enter upon the wholesale purchase of trucking companies across Canada with the taxpayers' money and thus jeopardize the interests of private trucking operators who are making a contribution to the country without any assistance from the taxpayer.
From time to time we have heard that the railways must get into the trucking business. At the present time the railways of Canada control the running rights from the east coast to the west coast and I do not believe this is fair competition with the trucking industry. I know that in Hamilton we have a great many independent trucking concerns who have made many complaints to me about this situation. With all due respect to the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Brunsden), I should like to point out to him that the independent trucking firms across the country have not come to the government of Canada asking for protection, subsidies, handouts or tax concessions. They have not asked for any of these things. All they have asked for is fair competition so that they in turn can operate their businesses.
I think the railways, especially the C.N.R. which has a vast amount of money at its command, are being most unfair in their attitude toward the trucking firms. I know they are exerting a great deal of pressure so that the independent trucking industry will not have the benefit of legislation such as is now before us. I might indicate certain ways in which they have done this. The C.N.R. and the C.P.R. have appointed as directors of their newly acquired trucking companies men who are also directors of the truckers associations in the various provinces, and every time this problem has come up at some of the association meetings the directors of these crown trucking firms have objected to the independent operators' plea for this type of legislation. I think it is very difficult to comprehend the power of the Canadian National Railways to work against the independent operators.
I will not mention the rate, but I know that the trucking rate from Burlington, Ontario to Calgary and Edmonton was fixed at

a certain figure. In the particular instance I have in mind the trucking firm was rendering a great service to the shipper. The trucking firm could go right to the loading dock of the company, transport the load out west and discharge it at the loading dock of the receiver at Edmonton or Calgary, whereas formerly the railway would not pick up the material at the loading dock. The persons shipping it had to take the material to the freight yards for loading on a car. The car was then taken to Calgary, sat in the yard there for a day and a half and some two or three days later the material was delivered.
The trucking firm provided a service whereby they went right to the loading dock of the company and took the material to the loading dock of the receiver in Calgary. I was dismayed to find out that the C.N.R. had bought a very large trucking firm that transported a considerable amount of goods from Burlington, Ontario, to Calgary and had cut some 78 cents a hundred off the rate. The firm that had been doing the job was very disturbed about this. They had had the contract for a great many years, and had secured it through fair competition. They submitted their tender, as did five or six other trucking companies, got the job, and found they were able to carry it out economically and make a fair return.
The C.N.R. came along and took this contract away from them for a certain period of time by cutting 78 cents a hundred off the rate on truckload lots. The firm that lost the contract told me that 78 cents off the rate would put their company about 20 per cent in the hole. I am trying to show that there is unfair competition.
I think it should also be pointed out that in the bill of the hon. member it is quite clear that all he wants to do is to give the trucking industry the right to appeal to the board of transport commissioners so that they can present their arguments there, protect themselves and keep competitive rates throughout the country in line. Then we will not find so many bankruptcies. I am not using the word "bankruptcy" to try to make it appear that the situation is more serious than it is. However, it is really very serious.
My understanding is that the C.N.R. has spent some $10 million to $20 million on the purchase of trucking industries throughout the country. The directors of the firms concerned are still acting as directors of these leasehold companies. I would be very interested in finding out whether in fact these subsidiaries are paying taxes. People can only pay taxes if they make money and we all know that the C.N.R. never makes any money. They are always in the hole and

coming to parliament to ask tor money. I would be very interested in finding out whether these subsidiaries of the C.N.R. that control trucking industries across the country are in fact paying taxes and are really in fair competition with the independent trucking companies. I wonder whether these subsidiaries are legitimate business in the same way as the independent operator who has to pay taxes.
I do not think railway monopolies are a good thing. The hon. member for Vancouver -Kingsway has proved many of his points by quoting from royal commission reports which indicate that free competition is necessary. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) indicated that royal commissions on maritime transportation felt that competition was necessary.
I think that the government must take action on this matter. I hope that the legislation will be passed. If there are other speakers who wish to speak I hope they will do so and impress upon the house and the government the need for action in this matter at this time. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) says that the government will act when the report of the royal commission on transportation is received. Some two and a half years ago when the C.N.R. first went into the trucking business people came to me, as they did to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, and told me just what would happen in Canada if the railways went into the trucking business. It is now taking place.
The C.N.R. first of all purchased one line from Toronto to Edmonton. Then they purchased another line from Montreal to Halifax. We find now that the C.N.R. and C.P.R. control the running rights from coast to coast and can arbitrarily set the rates at which they will transport products. We are subsidizing the railways to a great extent in my opinion and I simply want to make sure that the subsidy we give them is not going out through the back door to these leasehold companies in order to try to put the independent trucking operators out of business. I say again the trucking industry as a whole is not asking for protection, subsidies, tax considerations or anything like that. All the trucking industry desires is to be able to go to the board of transport commissioners for a fair hearing, and I hope that they can be given this opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak briefly on this bill. I do not intend to go into all the details connected with the bill. I offer my support of the measure in principle and to mention some of the important factors that make it necessary for us to keep a healthy road transportation system in Canada. I hope that

if it is not possible to have a vote on this measure tonight the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) will introduce it again in some form in the not too distant future so that we will be afforded an opportunity of doing something definite about this problem, because the bill has a good deal of merit.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) for introducing the bill at this time, and there is no better way in which I can do that than by supporting the principle of the bill. Road transportation by motor vehicles has become a very important part of our transportation system. This system has been developed principally by private enterprise and, over the years has developed into a very efficient system. It is rendering great service to Canada and strengthening our economy.
During the past 25 years we have seen a great many branch railway lines abandoned by order of the board of transport commissioners. I am not quarrelling with that. However in many instances industries in those areas were left without a means of transporting their goods from one place to another. Had it not been for the fact these independent trucking companies provided a service, many of these industries would have been forced to close down. The trucking industry, in some cases, is really the lifeline of secondary industry. That, in itself, is a most important factor and one which should compel us to do all we can to keep the industry stable and in a good financial position.
The two railway companies, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, are getting into the trucking business in a big way. Much of our mail and express is now transported by trucks owned by the two railway companies. This is the business of the railways, and there is nobody questioning their right to do so. However, when the railway companies enter into competition with private trucking companies, I think we should make sure that the private trucking companies are protected from unfair competition. None of us object to competition, and I am sure we do not object to the two railway companies entering the trucking business in a way that is fair and competitive. However, the great resources behind these two companies would enable them, if they wished to do so, to undercut the private companies to such an extent that the private companies may be forced out of business.
There is one service being built up in Canada today which I am very pleased to see. It is a service whereby the railways and the trucking companies work together. I refer to the piggyback service. The trucks are loaded on railway cars which transport them from one place to another. At one time it was

mostly the railways that participated in this service, but now the trucking companies all over Canada are taking advantage of it. I believe this is a place where the two transportation systems can co-operate for the benefit of Canada. We do not want to get into a situation in this country as they did in Great Britain a few years ago. Great Britain nationalized the road haulage transport system and it was turned over to the railway companies for operation. The railway companies ran it for only a few years, then it was turned back to private enterprise, at which time the system was in a rundown condition. This is another reason for keeping the road transportation system in Canada in the hands of free enterprise.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to give the independent trucking companies the right to appeal to the board of transport commissioners against unfair rate cutting. This does not give the trucking companies great powers or a means of exploiting the public. However, in my opinion, it is something that is becoming more important as time passes. We know that if a railway company in operating a branch line at a loss wishes to abandon a line or increase rates, It has to go to the board of transport commissioners for permission. The road transportation system as a part of our transportation system, deserves the same consideration so I heartily endorse this measure. As I say, I hope that if the bill does not receive approval at this time it will in the not too distant future. This is not a bill granting a monopoly to anyone. It is a bill to prevent the big railway companies from monopolizing a business which was built up by these independent trucking companies, built into a very efficient business, and we should do what we can to preserve their undertaking.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I erroneously said that we had not insured any sales to Cuba. What I should have said was that we had not financed any sales to Cuba, nor have we financed any sales to any communist country.
As hon. members opposite know, we have always insured sales to any country, including communist countries, from the time that the act was first put into force, in 1944; and during the term of office of the former government several millions of dollars of sales to communist countries were insured.
I shall be glad to table, when it arrives, a report which shows, by countries, the amount of insurance that has been issued for the 12 months as reported to the end of December, 1961.

Further to what I said this afternoon with respect to exports to Cuba, I have reconfirmed that no explosives of any strategic significance have been export licensed from Canada to Cuba.
I explained to the committee, in reply to a question regarding the agreed strategic materials list, that it is a classified document and I am unable to table it. Perhaps I may remind hon. members of what has been stated before in the house with respect to the establishment of the list of materials which are listed as strategic.
Hon. members will recall that there is an organization in Paris called COCOM. The initials stand for "Co-ordinating Committee". The purpose of this committee is to co-ordinate national policies on the strategic classification of materials. As far as control of materials is concerned, international trade is, to all intents and purposes, indivisible. If one country supplies what another refuses, control would be of no avail. There is therefore this arrangement for reaching agreement on what would be classified as strategic.
The governments which collaborate in COCOM are those of all the NATO countries, with the exception of Iceland, but with the addition of Japan. This is the group of countries which, in effect, sets the common standards of what are strategic materials. Canada and the United States are, of course, members of COCOM.
Everything on the strategic list established by COCOM is included within our export control list-a list which has been in existence for many years, as members opposite well know-which is amended from time to time.
Ordinary commercial grades of explosives such as those used for quarrying, road construction and other excavating purposes, are not included in the COCOM list nor are they included in our export control list, and when of Canadian origin may be exported without permit to any destination.
It is my understanding that no more than what might be regarded as small commercial shipments of such explosives have been made to Cuba.
I thought it advisable to give the committee this more detailed explanation. I am well aware that there is an extreme sensitivity on this subject in the United States, and that there has been a tendency apparent in the United States to exaggerate, and possibly misunderstand, press reports emanating from Canada regarding the type of trade which is being carried on with Cuba. We have satisfied ourselves from our own investigation that no arms and ammunition, or other goods

of recognized strategic significance, are moving in our trade with Cuba, and any inference to the contrary certainly tends to do Canada a disservice in our relations with our American friends.
As I have said, Mr. Chairman, I will table as soon as it arrives a list showing the countries for which we have insured exports during the past year and the monetary value of those shipments. The specific commodities in each case are not available for the moment. They will become available when the annual report of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation is made, I believe early next month. At that time the complete list of commodities will be made available. I am unable to present that information at this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING BUSINESS IMPROVEMENT LOANS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-49 to amend the Small Business Loans Act.
He said: The proposed amendment to the Small Businesses Loans Act will serve to broaden the terms of this legislation. Briefly, it is intended to add to the purposes for which guaranteed loans may now be made. In effect, the amendment makes provision for dealing with credit requirements of small enterprises for the purpose of relocating business premises.
Hon. members will recall that this legislation was introduced about a year ago to fill a gap in existing credit facilities. At that time, there was general agreement that proprietors of small businesses experienced difficulties in obtaining funds on suitable terms and conditions to finance capital improvements. The act was designed to alleviate this situation by providing that each bank be guaranteed against loss up to 10 per cent of the business improvement loans made by it. Such loans are now available for the purchase and improvement of equipment as well as the expansion and renovation of business premises. The maximum amount which may be borrowed by a small businessman is $25,000 and the maximum period of repayment runs for 10 years.
It gives me great pleasure and satisfaction to inform the house that notwithstanding the relatively short period during which the legislation has been in operation, the merits of this loan scheme have been clearly demonstrated. There is, in fact, tangible evidence of the sizeable assistance obtained by small business enterprises in all the provinces. I should like to say that the banks in carrying out the task of administering the scheme have acted in an effective and co-operative manner and deserve a large share of the credit for the results achieved to date.
From the inception of the act in January 1961 to the end of last December, 2,977 loans amounting to over $25.5 million were made to small business enterprises. Out of total loan disbursements, service businesses accounted for about one half, retail establishments for

Small Businesses Loans Act about one quarter, manufacturers for about one fifth and the remainder of the loans went to wholesalers. The average size of individual loans was around $8,600. To conclude this review, I should point out that during the period from April to the end of December when the initial difficulties of operating the loan scheme had been overcome, lending took place at an annual rate of about $32 million. There is every reason to expect that this level will rise substantially as more and more small businessmen become familiar with the facilities provided under the act.
Of course, developments in the field of business improvement loans were kept under constant review by the government. Although progress under the legislation has been gratifying, the experience gained from operations during the past year indicates that there is one area where a broadening of the terms of the legislation would provide a useful additional measure of assistance to small business. Specifically, the act in its present form does not provide authority to finance the acquisition of business premises at an alternative location and this has led to some disappointment among potential borrowers, for example, in cases where relocation is forced on a proprietor because zoning regulations do not permit him to expand his existing premises. Accordingly, it is intended to make business improvement loans available for the purpose of financing the construction or the purchase of premises at an alternative site. In detail, proprietors of small business enterprises will be eligible for relocation loans not only in those instances where the premises at the present site cease to be available, but also in cases where relocation makes sense as a sound business proposition.
In introducing the small businesses loans legislation at the last session of parliament, I referred to the important role played by small business within the framework of the Canadian economy and I expressed the hope that the act would be instrumental in furthering the efficiency and competitive strength of small business enterprises. As indicated, there is every reason to believe that the new credit facilities can make a significant contribution towards achieving this objective. No doubt, the proposed amendment will prove useful in rounding out the assistance available to small business and will help to ensure the sound development of this important sector of the Canadian economy.

Mr. Speaker, I was reminding the house that in November of 1960 the government introduced a bill relating to credit for small business. Small Businesses Loans Act passed the legislative recommendations brought forward by the government.
Four weeks after the House of Commons had done its job it became apparent that the cabinet had not done its homework. Hon. gentlemen who make up the cabinet did not have ready the regulations under which the commercial banks of this country could extend credit until January 19, 1961. This is what happened despite the fact that in the election campaign of 1957 the great messiah of the Conservative party was stating publicly that we must make available for small business lending opportunities similar to those available in the United States. Speaking in Brockville in May of 1957 the present Prime Minister referred to 35,000 small manufacturing concerns across this country which were not receiving the credit facilities to which they were entitled.
As reported in the Ottawa Citizen of May 9, 1957 the hon. gentleman increased that figure. He referred, according to the press, to 37,400 manufacturing establishments in Canada employing 99 persons or less that should be entitled to better credit opportunities.
That was the position taken by the Prime Minister in 1957. The Conservative government did not introduce this legislation until November 1960. I say that the executive of the country had not done their homework. They had not even thought out this matter in advance. Although parliament unanimously approved the legislation early in December the regulations under which the improvements would be made available to the commercial banks were not introduced until January 19.
The results have been dismal. No such provision appears in the bill that is before us.
There is no broadening of the definitions except for the purpose of permitting a business improvement loan to be made for construction on an alternative site. That is all that is in this bill. Hon. members know that if there was anything of consequence involving increased expenditures on the part of

Small Businesses Loans Act
this administration under this legislation this bill would have been preceded by a resolution.
