The bill has been in operation only a short time. However, from my own experience, in talking to certain persons in my own constituency, may I say that I think it has been of some benefit. I think there is some justification for the criticisms made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, (Mr. Benidickson) namely that the act is not quite as imaginative and good as it might be. In view of the experience of the operation of the act I suggest that the minister consider bringing in some further amendments to widen its application and to make it even more useful.
I am very much interested in this measure. It has been brought to my attention that it has been of some value to small industry in my district and to small businessmen and merchants, and that in some cases persons wishing to provide services on a small scale in small communities found this act beneficial in getting started. I refer to the solid type of citizen who has property, character and ability but has not the required money. Under these circumstances I think this act has been of some benefit.
I notice that it has been of benefit to the tourist industry in my constituency in getting funds from the banks for the erection of fishing camps and tourist cabins and for the improvement of facilities connected with resorts and so on. I have had one or two cases of those engaged in fur farming having taken advantage of this act. To my knowledge there is one case of a man who has undertaken a small boat building industry, just a one-man or two-man show, and who has taken advantage of the act. I am very keen on this matter of promoting the small scale industry and the small scale business in the local community, inasmuch as the society in which we are living at the present time is actually destroying free enterprise of all kinds, with the large scale development of monopoly capitalism.
I notice that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) is listening very carefully and that up to a certain point he seemed to agree with me. However, I do not think he altogether agrees with my analysis of what is happening in modern society. Nevertheless, I feel very keenly about that matter.
When the minister speaks, I wish to ask him whether he thinks this act will also apply to trappers. We have some trapping industries operating quite extensively in the constituency in which I live. We have good trappers who are licensed to operate in the district. Some of them have trap lines which

are 50 miles long and they get from $3,000 to $10,000 worth of furs in a winter. But sometimes a young man commencing wishes to get a set of traps and to build a line. When the minister replies I should like him to tell the house whether this legislation would apply to such a person wishing to engage in the trapping business; I refer to a small business.
While the act has been in operation for only a short time the experience with it has proved the necessity for this amendment. We have noticed the same thing with a good number of pieces of legislation that have been brought before the house. It is something that is normal and I am always pleased to see it. I am glad to see governments amend acts as a result of the experience in their operations.
I might say that one thing which has been brought to my attention on several occasions during the last year, particularly by persons engaged in the tourist business or summer resort business is that they could not take advantage of the act because they wanted to relocate cabins, certain facilities or things of that sort. I understand that this amendment would make it possible for these people to relocate on more suitable sites, to develop other sites and so on. Strangely enough, only this morning I received a very lengthy letter from a businessman who was engaged in the tourist industry. Mr. Speaker, it took the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) a year to realize that the members of the opposition were right, in November 1960, when the bill on loans to small businesses was submitted and when we claimed that such legislation would not give enough assistance to small businessmen.

Small Businesses Loans Act
The amendment to the Small Businesses Loans Act submitted tonight was suggested during the debate on the bill in November
1960,	but as usual, the minister ignored that suggestion like all the others that are made by opposition members.
When that piece of legislation was introduced,	it	was heartily welcomed	by	allmembers	of	this house. But as for	us,	onthis side,	we	asked for a broadening	of	theact. We also	made some suggestions	with a
view to giving further assistance to small businessmen.
The minister in his majesty ignored all the suggestions made. He uttered high-sounding sentences, as he is wont to, wishing to give the impression that he could save the small enterprise from disaster.
He predicted, as recorded in Hansard of November 21, 1960, that the owners of small enterprises would rush to the banks to borrow. Indeed, he forecast that, during the winter months following the adoption of the act loans would amount to $75 million. That amount would not only help small business enterprises, but check unemployment.
The minister was so enthusiastic about what he believed was his masterpiece that he had even fixed at $300 million the total amount of loans that the banks would grant and which would be guaranteed by the government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what has been the actual result of that legislation? On November 30,
1961,	after the act had been in force for a year, out of a potential of some 400,000 small enterprises, as defined by the act, only 2,737 loans had been granted by the banks, for a total amount of $23 million.
In view of the needs of small business and the insignificant number of loans granted, as well as the ridiculous amount of those loans as compared to the minister's forecast there is ground for some questioning. The minister would be well advised to think seriously and say to himself that he would have been wise to show some humility, for once, and admit that he should have followed certain suggestions made to him by members of the opposition when he introduced his bill on November 21, 1960.
If the results have been disappointing, both for the government and for the small business enterprises, it is because the act was neither satisfactory nor adequate.
First of all, the act does nothing more than guarantee bank loans to the extent of 10 per cent. Therefore, of the $23 million granted in loans as of November 30, 1961,


under the act, the government actually guaranteed only an amount of $2.3 million to the banks.
Under the circumstances, the banks, which are not charitable institutions by nature, continued as before to follow practically the same policy towards the small businessmen who applied for loans.
Besides, is it not the powerful Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) who stated, not before architects this time, but in this house on November 22, 1960, as reported on page 1 of the appendix of Hansard of that date:
It must be realized that in some cases, banks have been forced, quite against their will, to turn down applications from people who were seeking funds to expand their businesses.
Well, according to the number and amount of bank loans made under the act, banks have kept on turning down applications in a proportion of 90 per cent since, under the act, loans are guaranteed only on the basis of 10 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, the bill under consideration is a slight improvement. It has taken the minister over a year to introduce it. At that rate, small businessmen will have the time to disappear from the economic scene before we have legislation broad enough to be truly useful to them.
All hon. members will agree that small enterprises are of vital importance to our economy. Under such circumstances, it is the duty of the government to look after the problems of the wholesaler, the small manufacturer, the contractor, the provider of services, the retailer and so on.
The very existence and the survival of the small business enterprise in Canada is a vital element in our free society. Without the small business enterprise, we would have less free enterprise and more state control.
It is generally recognized that, in the past few years, the small business enterprise has found it increasingly difficult to stay alive.
The main difficulties of the small businessman, of the small merchant, of the small manufacturer, have been the lack of capital, the difficulty encountered in obtaining credit at a reasonable rate, the lack of research facilities and unfair competition, such as restrictions imposed by big business.
It is of the utmost necessity that the government take the required steps to abolish these obstacles which stand in the way of the small enterprise, and that it take them immediately. Otherwise, people will say the same thing Mr. Andre Laurendeau said about

another measure announced in the house, a few days ago, by the Minister of Finance: "Too little and too late."
Of course, all groups in this house were pleased with the introduction of the bill on small business loans, all hon. members supported that measure and voted for it. But it must be recalled that the members of the opposition claimed that to be really effective and to achieve its aims, the act should be extended.
This amendment to the act which is before us meets a suggestion made by the opposition on the introduction of the bill. Its purpose is to permit a business improvement loan for the construction or purchase of alternative premises where the premises in which the enterprise was or is being carried on are no longer available or will cease to be available for that purpose.
It is a welcome improvement, but it is not
enough.
Whatever the Associate Minister of National Defence may think, bankers will continue to turn down requests from small business owners, as they have been doing, since they only have a 10 per cent guarantee.
And the minister, with child-like hope, is just as satisfied with the poor results obtained as with the collapsing of his nice forecast.
Instead of introducing that amendment only, the minister should have also amended the law in order to enable small businessmen to obtain working capital. Instead of leaving the owners with only one alternative, that of borrowing and running into debt, which may be necessary when one is in business, the government should adopt the same graduated scale of income tax for small businesses as for individuals. Thus, the small businessman would be relieved of a burden which would leave him more money available for his business.
The legislation should also place areas where unemployment is prevalent in a special category. In those communities, special attention should be given to the businessmen who want to start a small business. Easier credit should be made available to them. This would provide a way of relieving unemployment in the smaller communities and to check its growth in the cities, for the unemployed would not be tempted to leave the smaller communities for the big cities.
Mr. Speaker, these are a few comments I wanted to submit on this question which is so important for our economy: assistance to small businesses.
For the time being, I support the amendment which is brought forward, but I regret that the government does not go further. The
Small Businesses Loans Act country will need a Liberal government so that the small enterprise may be treated in all fairness.
